cells.tense: You are putting a true feeling into plain words right now, and the words are landing on the person you aimed them at.
cells.act: calibrate what you say to what can be heard
cells.ask: Pick the one true sentence you have been holding back from a person. Measure it against what they can take in this week, trim to the shortest form that still reaches them, and say it that way — once.
cells.core:
You can say a hard thing and have it land. The feeling is real, the words are picked for the person hearing them, and after it the two of you are still talking to each other. That is this going well, and you can feel it when a conversation moves because the sentence was true rather than loud.

So measure the sentence before it leaves you. The honest version is not the heaviest one; the one that works is the honest version this person can hold. Say less than you want to, at the size they can take, and stop there — no second pass, no re-explaining the point, no checking that it arrived. What you hand them is a thing they can carry home.
cells.sheetLine: True, sized to the person, said once.
cells.verb: moving a shared feeling or practice through people until it changes
cells.place: in the place where things between people get weighed and set right

cells.tense: You will be forcing the change through before the people near you have agreed it needs to happen.
cells.act: move the structure one real inch
cells.ask: Choose the thing between you and someone else that you can't wait to set right. Make one real move, then stop with the next one unplanned, and keep your hands off it until they answer.
cells.core:
You can see how things between people ought to run, and you are sure one good push gets them there. So the push comes early, and the change itself is right, and it lands like something done to the room instead of with it — ahead of where the other person is standing.

One move at a time is the technique. Make the single move toward what you believe is fair, then leave a gap wide enough for the other side to get their hands on it before you make the next. What carries you is that you don't quit; the version of that which brings another person along is slower than you would pick. What gets built that way holds up because their hands are under it too.
cells.sheetLine: Force it through and you'll be holding it alone.
cells.verb: moving a shared feeling or practice through people until it changes
cells.place: in the place where things between people get weighed and set right

cells.tense: You have your own end of the scale in hand and set it down on the far side of a door.
cells.act: cut to the logic and act on it
cells.ask: Take the unfair situation between people that you have gone quiet about. Strip it to the bare line of who gave and who owes — no feelings on the page — and make the next step that line calls for.
cells.core:
You can see when things between people are out of proportion. What has stopped is the moving of the scale — you sit near it, busy with other work, and the unfair thing waits where it is. The weight sits there unweighed and the ones it touches know it.

Reason, in private, all the way to the cold line: who gave, who took, what would sit level. Once the line is sharp you reach the sharp point of it, and the step after that is small. Nothing has to convince you — the logic is already in the sentence. Do the one thing the line requires, or say it plainly to the person it concerns, and then let it be done.
cells.sheetLine: You have the logic. Make the move.

cells.tense: You are evening things out between people while your own account shows someone who stays clear of it.
cells.act: tell the truth with care for when and how
cells.ask: Notice where you shifted the balance without saying so — a fact softened, a word held back, a weight lifted off someone. Tell that truth at a size that can be heard, then let it stand where it lands.
cells.core:
The balance between people holds because you keep it holding — a detail left out so someone can rest, a truth given a softer edge, a small thing carried for another without being asked. Ask you about it and the story you'd tell is of someone standing at the edge, uninvolved.

Tell one piece of the truth, at a size that can be heard, while the telling still helps. Then leave it — no walking it back, no explaining why you said it, no checking on how it landed. What you keep back is a kindness, and it costs you the part where you are one of the people at the table instead of the one managing it. The one who tempers can also speak plainly.
